hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever had a night where you just couldn’t stop wrestling with something?
options: then this story is for you. listen.
then you’ll recognize this man. listen.
good. keep this one for the night you do.

steps.line: Twenty years earlier, Jacob had tricked his twin brother Esau out of their father’s blessing, and run. Now he was coming home. Esau was coming too, with four hundred men.
That night, Jacob sent his family and everything he had across the river Jabbok. He stayed behind, alone, in the dark.

steps.q: In the dark, someone grabs Jacob, and they wrestle until dawn. Who, in the Torah’s own words?
steps.why: The Torah says only “a man” (Genesis 32:25). The prophet Hosea later calls him an angel, and the rabbis offered more answers. The story itself keeps it open.

steps.line: And a man wrestled with him until the break of dawn. No name. No warning. Just the two of them in the dust, all night long.
As dawn came, the stranger touched Jacob’s hip and wrenched it. “Let me go,” he said. Jacob answered, “I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.”

steps.q: Before blessing him, the stranger asks, “What is your name?” Why might that question sting?
o: He was ashamed of his father
He had sworn to keep it secret
steps.why: Jacob means “heel,” and sounds like “he cheats.” Esau had said as much. Saying it out loud meant owning who he had been.

steps.q: Jacob won’t let go without a blessing. What do you think the blessing is?
steps.why: A new name. In the Torah, a new name marks a new person. Abram became Abraham the same way.

steps.line: The blessing was a new name. “No more Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
Jacob named the place Peniel, “the face of God.” The sun rose as he crossed over, and he was limping. Hurt, and renamed, in the same morning.

steps.q: Jacob walks away limping, and the Torah still calls the night a blessing. What is the story saying?
o: The limp was his punishment for tricking Esau
A struggle can leave a wound and a blessing
Jacob lost the fight, but was forgiven
steps.why: He held on, and he prevailed. The limp didn’t cancel the blessing. Both came out of the same night.

steps.q: Limping, Jacob finally meets Esau and his four hundred men. What does Esau do?
o: Runs to hug him, and they weep
steps.why: Genesis 33: Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, kissed him, and they wept. The night of wrestling ended in a brother’s arms.

steps.line: Today, the Jewish people are still called the children of Israel: named for a man who wrestled all night, and held on.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. the jewish people aren’t named for someone who never doubted. they’re named for someone who wrestled all night and held on.
and the torah never says who the stranger was. a man? an angel? jewish teachers have kept more than one answer. some nights, you can’t tell who you’re wrestling with.

steps.q: Because of Jacob’s hip, kosher law forbids one sinew in the hind leg. Removing it is slow work. So outside Israel, kosher butchers usually…
o: Sell the hindquarter to regular shops
Charge double for the back legs
Serve hip meat only at Passover
steps.why: The rule comes straight from this night (Genesis 32:33). Taking out the sinew takes real skill, so the back half, sirloin and all, usually goes to non-kosher butchers. One night’s limp still shapes the menu.

today.say: think of one struggle you’re in right now. today, write down one thing it has given you, next to what it has cost. jacob walked away with both: a limp, and a new name.
options: the mark and the blessing, side by side. that’s israel.
that’s okay. jacob wrestled all night before the blessing came.

tomorrow.title: We will do, and we will hear.
tomorrow.line: a mountain shakes, a horn grows louder, and a whole people gives an answer the rabbis never stopped talking about.
